newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ICRC says kept to rules in Peru hostage drama.
newsitem.headline: ICRC says kept to rules in Peru hostage drama.

text.p: The Swiss-run International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said on Monday it had stuck firmly to its mandate as a "neutral intermediary" during the long-running hostage crisis in Peru.

Senior officials of the humanitarian organisation told a news conference they hoped the ICRC could shortly resume visits to some 350 left-wing prisoners held in Peruvian jails which were barred when the drama began last December 17.
"I think we followed to the letter what our mandate required us to do throughout the affair. We were totally transparent with all sides," ICRC director for the Americas Francis Amar said.

"Our role was as a neutral intermediary on humanitarian issues," said Michel Minnig, head of the ICRC office in Lima and a key figure through much of the drama in and around the Japanese ambassador's residence in the Peruvian capital.

The crisis began when guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) seized the residence during a diplomatic reception and held 72 hostages after releasing most of their original captives, including Minnig.

It ended on April 22 when Peruvian troops stormed the building in an operation in which all 14 guerrillas and two soldiers were killed and one hostage, a senior Peruvian judge, died in hospital. All the other hostages survived.
Minnig and Amar said they had no direct information to confirm reports that some of the guerrillas were captured and then killed by the soldiers.
"We are very concerned at these reports," Amar said. "We are studying all the information available and then we will decide what to do.
"But if we were to make any intervention with the Peruvian authorities, it would be confidential, in conformity with our rules."
Amar said that despite the effective expulsion of Minnig's deputy, Juan-Pedro Scherer, near the end of the crisis, the ICRC itself appeared to retain the confidence of the Lima government.
"Even when they were telling us Juan-Pedro was not acting in conformity with his mission, they repeated that they had full confidence in our organisation," he told the news conference.
He said Peruvian officials had accused Scherer, an Argentine-born Swiss citizen, of spending too much time with the guerrillas in the residence and being too friendly with them.

"We told them that the ICRC could not carry out its mission without being in good contact with both sides....We would have expected a better explanation from them on such an important issue," declared Amar.
